title: Well-quasi-ordering Eulerian digraphs by weak immersion
formal:
Is the class of all finite Eulerian directed multigraphs well-quasi-ordered by weak immersion?

Let \(\mathcal E\) be the set of graphs defined below: loops and parallel arcs are allowed, and every vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree. No connectivity, degree, width or surface-embedding restriction is imposed. Write \(H\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{wi}}G\) when \(H\) has a weak immersion in \(G\), with directions and distinct arc identities respected.

The exact proposition is
\[
\forall (G_i)_{i\in\mathbb N}\in\mathcal E^{\mathbb N}\quad
\exists i,j\in\mathbb N\quad
i<j\ \land\ G_i\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{wi}}G_j,
\]
where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The sequence is arbitrary and need not be computable. The earlier graph must immerse in the later graph in the order specified by the sequence. This is Conjecture 3.2 of the ICALP 2026 source, with the graph and immersion conventions supplied by its full version.
why: A positive answer would extend a central type of structural graph-ordering theorem to the broad Eulerian directed setting. It would imply finite forbidden-immersion descriptions for properties closed under weak immersion within that class, with the fixed-property testing consequences explained by the source. General digraphs and strong immersions admit known ordering obstructions, so the balance condition and the precise weak relation are substantive. A counterexample would identify a fundamental obstruction that survives both restrictions.
status_note: The inspected ICALP 2026 publication, released 1 July 2026, explicitly states this unrestricted target as Conjecture 3.2, and its 8 May full version specifies the model. The established theorem scopes reviewed here impose width or degree restrictions. A 10 March 2026 author seminar abstract expressed belief in proofs of the general conjectures, but no complete general proof was available there or found in the bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026; the later inspected papers still label this statement a conjecture. Scientific status is therefore uncertain rather than treated as a verified resolution. This review checks formulation and theorem scope, not all literature or Lean proofs.

importance.reason: A broad structural ordering conjecture for a central directed graph class, with finite-obstruction and fixed-property testing consequences. It addresses a substantial boundary between the known undirected immersion theory, failures for unrestricted digraphs, and failures for strong immersion even on Eulerian digraphs. The unrestricted statement is more consequential than any one bounded-width case. This individual assessment replaces the provisional unassessed midpoint and does not depend on the publication venue or certify a general proof announcement.

sentences: An Eulerian digraph is a finite directed multigraph with equal incoming and outgoing arc counts at every vertex, allowing loops, parallel arcs and disconnected components.
A weak immersion represents vertices injectively and arcs by arc-disjoint directed trails, which may meet at vertices and pass through other represented vertices.
The conjecture says that every infinite sequence of these digraphs contains an earlier graph weakly immersed in a later graph.
The inspected 2026 results establish restricted width and degree cases, while a general proof announcement has not been verified in the available sources.
A complete Lean answer must prove the unrestricted sequence statement or give one infinite sequence with no qualifying earlier-to-later pair.

definitions:
For a nonnegative integer \(n\), let \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite directed multigraph is a tuple
\[
G=(n,m,\operatorname{tail}_G,\operatorname{head}_G),
\qquad
\operatorname{tail}_G,\operatorname{head}_G:[m]\to[n],
\]
where \(n,m\) are nonnegative integers. Write \(V(G)\) for its vertex set, a copy of \([n]\), and \(E(G)\) for its arc set, a separate copy of \([m]\). If \(n=0\), necessarily \(m=0\). An arc \(e\) is directed from \(\operatorname{tail}_G(e)\) to \(\operatorname{head}_G(e)\). The two endpoints may be equal, giving a loop. Distinct arcs may have identical ordered endpoints, giving parallel arcs. Oppositely directed arcs are also permitted. Arc identities are distinct even when endpoints coincide.

For a vertex \(v\), define
\[
\deg_G^+(v)=
|\{e\in[m]:\operatorname{tail}_G(e)=v\}|,\qquad
\deg_G^-(v)=
|\{e\in[m]:\operatorname{head}_G(e)=v\}|.
\]
Each loop contributes one to each degree, and parallel arcs are counted separately. The graph is Eulerian when
\[
\forall v\in[n]\quad \deg_G^+(v)=\deg_G^-(v).
\]
This degree-balance definition does not require weak or strong connectivity. Isolated vertices, edgeless graphs and the empty graph are included. Let \(\mathcal E\) be the set of all such tuples satisfying this condition. Numbering vertices and arcs is only a finite representation; immersion maps need not preserve the numbers.

A nonempty directed trail in \(G\) from \(u\) to \(v\) is a list of pairwise distinct arcs
\[
P=(a_1,\ldots,a_\ell),\qquad \ell\ge1,
\]
such that
\[
\operatorname{tail}_G(a_1)=u,\qquad
\operatorname{head}_G(a_\ell)=v,\qquad
\operatorname{head}_G(a_r)=\operatorname{tail}_G(a_{r+1})
\quad(1\le r<\ell).
\]
Vertices may be visited repeatedly. The endpoints may coincide; in that case the trail is closed and still uses at least one arc. Write \(E(P)=\{a_1,\ldots,a_\ell\}\). Its internal vertex occurrences are the vertices \(\operatorname{head}_G(a_r)\) for \(1\le r<\ell\), including any that equal an endpoint. Two trails are arc-disjoint when their arc sets are disjoint. They may share vertices.

A weak immersion of \(H\) in \(G\) consists of an injective vertex map
\[
\phi:V(H)\to V(G)
\]
and, for every arc \(e\in E(H)\), a nonempty directed trail \(P_e\) in \(G\) from \(\phi(\operatorname{tail}_H(e))\) to \(\phi(\operatorname{head}_H(e))\), such that
\[
\forall e,f\in E(H),\ e\ne f
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E(P_e)\cap E(P_f)=\varnothing.
\]
There is no additional restriction on internal vertices. In particular, a trail may pass through \(\phi(w)\) for another vertex \(w\) of \(H\), and different trails may meet at vertices. A loop of \(H\) must be represented by a nonempty closed directed trail at its image vertex; it cannot disappear into a route of length zero. Parallel arcs of \(H\) require separate arc-disjoint trails. The notation \(H\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{wi}}G\) means that such data exist.

The full source calls these trails “paths”; the definition here spells out its allowance for repeated vertices. A strong immersion would additionally forbid every internal vertex of every \(P_e\) from lying in \(\phi(V(H))\). That additional prohibition is not part of the target.

A quasi-order is a reflexive and transitive relation. It is a well-quasi-order when every infinite sequence has an earlier element related to a later one. The weak immersion relation above is the graph-containment relation used in the displayed proposition. An infinite sequence here is any function from \(\mathbb N\) to \(\mathcal E\); graphs may repeat, and the sequence has no prescribed degree, size or width bound. The question is a structural existence statement, with no algorithmic running-time requirement.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed well-quasi-ordering proposition or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must cover every infinite sequence in \(\mathcal E\) and establish indices \(i<j\) together with the existence of a direction-preserving injective vertex map and the required mutually arc-disjoint nonempty trails. It must retain loops, parallel arcs, isolated vertices and the absence of a connectivity assumption. No uniform algorithm selecting the indices or immersion is required.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists (G_i)_{i\in\mathbb N}\in\mathcal E^{\mathbb N}\quad
\forall i,j\in\mathbb N\quad
i<j\ \Longrightarrow\
\neg(G_i\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{wi}}G_j).
\]
This requires one infinite sequence of finite balanced digraphs and a proof excluding every qualifying weak immersion for every earlier-to-later pair. A mathematically specified sequence with a proof of these properties is sufficient; no computability requirement is added.

An infinite antichain for strong immersion alone does not refute this statement, because weak immersions may use represented vertices internally. A result only for bounded degree, bounded width, connected graphs, loopless graphs or a fixed surface class establishes the target only together with a proof covering the rest of the stated class. A finite collection of incomparable examples does not establish the negative proposition. This is an exact yes/no structural question; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not replace the complete Lean proof.

context_blocks.text: The full version treats digraphs as finite incidence structures with loops and parallel arcs, and explicitly defines Eulerian by degree balance without imposing connectivity. It also allows immersed arcs to follow directed trails with repeated vertices. The card retains these conventions.

The ICALP 2026 paper states the unrestricted weak-immersion claim as Conjecture 3.2. It separately shows that Eulerian digraphs are not well-quasi-ordered by strong immersion, even under strong restrictions on their underlying undirected graphs; that result does not refute this weaker containment relation.

Theorem 4.6 establishes well-quasi-ordering by strong immersion when carving width is bounded across the class. Carving width measures the largest arc cut in a tree arrangement of the vertices, and this bounded-width condition is absent from the conjecture.

Theorem 4.10 gives another partial result for weak immersion: bounded treewidth with at most one vertex above a fixed degree threshold. This still restricts the graphs and leaves the general conjecture as a separate target.
The September 2025 preprint on surface embeddings already states the general weak-immersion conjecture as Conjecture 1.7. Its surface and width results concern restricted graph classes.

A March 2026 author seminar abstract expressed belief in proofs of the general conjectures. The later inspected May full version and July ICALP publication continue to state the unrestricted weak-immersion result as a conjecture; the announcement is not treated here as a verified resolution.

Downloaded actual publisher eulerian-wqo-icalp2026.pdf/.txt, 19 pages. Read PDF pp. 1–9 for the graph relation, Eulerian convention, counterexample, general conjecture and applications; read Theorems 4.6–4.7 on p. 13 and Theorem 4.10 on p. 17. Publisher metadata gives 1 July 2026. The paper’s §4.1 warns that some technical definitions are simplified in the short version, so the complete graph and immersion definitions were recovered from its referenced full version instead of silently guessing.

Downloaded actual eulerian-wqo-full2026.pdf/.txt, arXiv:2605.07468v1, 8 May 2026. §2.2, PDF pp. 7–8, explicitly allows finite vertex and edge incidence sets, parallel arcs and loops. Eulerian means equality of incoming and outgoing arc counts and explicitly imposes no connectivity restrictions. Each loop counts once in each degree. The labeled [n]/[m] representation in the draft merely makes this set-sized for sequence quantification; the labels and their order do not constrain immersion maps. Empty/edgeless graphs and isolated vertices are not excluded by the source definition.

Full Definition 2.4 on PDF p. 8 uses paths to mean edge-nonrepeating directed sequences, with potentially repeated vertices and coincident endpoints. Full Definition 2.12 on p. 10 maps every arc to one such sequence, with disjoint arc sets, correct direction and injective branch vertices. Its immediate remark explicitly treats loops through closed routes. The draft calls these directed trails to avoid the standard simple-path ambiguity, and makes their nonempty length explicit: the source defines first and last edges, which requires at least one arc. A zero-length image of a loop is not permitted.

A trail may internally contain any branch vertex, including an endpoint that it revisits. This is weak immersion. The strong restriction is precisely that all internal vertices avoid the whole image of V(H). The source’s counterexample in Observation 2.1/Corollary 2.2 concerns strong immersion only, and the article explicitly notes it is not a weak-immersion antichain. The draft does not silently change to vertex-disjoint paths, strong immersion, butterfly minors, loopless digraphs or ordinary undirected graphs.

The target is forall infinite sequences exists i<j with G_i weakly immersing in G_j. Its full negative is one infinite sequence with no such earlier-to-later pair. Arbitrarily many finite examples or one strong-immersion antichain is insufficient. Computability of a negative sequence or an effective selector for the positive case is not required by the source and is not added. Reflexivity and transitivity of the actual relation are recorded in full Observation 2.15, PDF p. 11; the draft uses the concrete sequence formulation directly.

Partial-result scopes were checked in the actual publisher PDF. Theorem 4.6, p. 13, proves strong WQO for classes with a uniform carving-width bound; Theorem 4.7 describes the bounded-treewidth/bounded-degree setting. Theorem 4.10, p. 17, proves weak WQO with bounded treewidth and at most one vertex whose degree exceeds a fixed even threshold. Neither yields the general conjecture by dropping a fixed bound. Public progress states theorem scopes without reproducing construction methods or the source’s suggested strategies.
